newsitem.title: USA: US derivatives disclosure plans not helpful - survey.
newsitem.headline: US derivatives disclosure plans not helpful - survey.

text.p: Most U.S. corporations do not believe proposals by the Securities and Exchange Commission to enhance disclosure of derivatives holdings would improve investors' understanding of the risks involved, according to a new survey of companies.

About 50 percent of 319 public and private companies surveyed said investor understanding would improve "not at all" if the companies reported current values of derivatives, off-balance-sheet financial instruments whose value changes in conjunction with other instruments, commodities or price indexes, the survey by the Treasury Management Association found.
Another 30 percent said the reporting would help "to a small extent," while fewer than 20 percent said it would help "to a moderate extent" or more.

The association, a group representing more than 8,000 treasury officials, conducted the survey over the summer and released preliminary results at a conference of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association here on Wednesday.
Many firms also said in the survey that the SEC's proposed disclosure scheme did not accurately describe most of their financial risk management activities.
About 17 percent said the descriptions were "not at all" accurate, and another 35 percent said they were accurate "to a small extent."
About 33 percent said the requirements would describe their activities accurately "to a moderate extent," and 14 percent said "to a great extent or more."

The SEC offered firms three possible methods for reporting on derivatives activities: transactions listed in tabular form, an analysis of positions' sensitivity to various market moves, and use of quantitative figures such as "value at risk."

Surveyed firms said all three choices would be costly. About 54 percent said tabular presentation would involve a moderate or great added expense, while about 46 percent said it would be a minor or small incremental expense.
Some 79 percent said sensitivity analysis would involve a moderate or great expense, and 89 percent said "value at risk" would be a moderate or great expense.

Larger firms in the survey said they already make some derivatives disclosures. For firms with at least $1 billion in revenues, 83 percent report notes on derivatives use, though not all firms disclosed the notional amount of derivatives used or stated whether the instruments were held for trading or other purposes.
